title: How Coffins Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore coffins and caskets: what a coffin is for (a barrier between body and ground), the casket vs. coffin distinction in the US versus Britain and Australia, funeral industry language and economics, the rise and decline of metal caskets, cremation's effect on the casket trade, low-cost options from Walmart and Costco, the San Francisco Six Under club, protective "burping" coffins and exploding coffin syndrome, grave robbing and mort safes, global traditions (Ghana fantasy coffins, Bo people hanging coffins, Egyptian coffin texts and Book of the Dead), 19th-century safety coffins and fear of premature burial (taphephobia), expensive caskets such as the Promethean, DIY coffin plans, and a listener email from Peter about cancer scans and listening to the show.

entities.name: Premature Burial and How It May Be Prevented

segments.title: Opening banter and what makes a coffin
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about green burial and death topics, then define a coffin as a barrier between the body and the ground, noting a shroud is a very poor coffin.

segments.title: Coffin vs. casket and funeral home language
segments.summary: The word coffin comes from Greek and Latin roots. Americans say casket while Britain and Australia say coffin. Funeral homes avoid the word coffin, and casket shapes differ: caskets are rectangular with a split lid, coffins are hexagonal.

segments.title: Carpenter undertakers and the word pall
segments.summary: In the nineteenth century, local carpenters built coffins and often conducted funerals, which explains the word undertaker. The phrase cast a pall refers to a dark cloth placed over a casket.

segments.title: Casket industry, metal caskets, and cremation's impact
segments.summary: Caskets were once made by furniture companies such as Batesville. Metal caskets became popular after the Korean War and were highly profitable and expensive to tool up for. The casket industry declined as medicine reduced deaths and cremation rose from the 1980s. Oversized Goliath caskets are also made.

segments.title: Cheap caskets, rental caskets, and retail options
segments.summary: Cremation caskets can be cheap cardboard, and rental caskets are used for showy services. Walmart and Costco sell caskets, with a Our Lady of Guadalupe model priced differently at each store.

segments.title: Six Under club in San Francisco
segments.summary: The hosts describe a San Francisco club where couples can lie in a coffin and be buried while a night-vision webcam is projected on the club walls. Listeners can email to reserve space.

segments.title: Protective coffins, gas buildup, and exploding coffin syndrome
segments.summary: Sealed protective coffins with rubber gaskets trap gas from anaerobic decay, causing methane buildup. Exploding coffin syndrome was seen in mausoleums, and burping coffins were developed to vent gas. Companies cannot legally claim permanent protection.

segments.title: Coffin materials, public health rules, and regional differences
segments.summary: Coffins are made of wood, metal, fiberglass, bronze, clay, or stone depending on region. Linings are usually fabric like taffeta or velvet with batting. Public health rules and groundwater concerns mean most burials use concrete or cement vaults. Black coffins and wood finishes are discussed.

segments.title: Grave robbing, mort safes, and funeral costs
segments.summary: Early nineteenth-century body snatching supplied medical research. Protections included locked mausoleums, guarded graves, mort safes (iron cages set in concrete), and heavy planks or rocks in backfill. Average 2009 funeral cost was $6,560 and average metal casket $2,295. Funeral homes mark up caskets.

segments.title: Global coffin traditions: Ghana, Bo people, Egypt
segments.summary: Ghana has brightly colored, shaped coffins honoring the deceased's life. The Bo people of Sichuan hung coffins on cliffs. Ancient Egyptian coffin texts and the Book of the Dead describe the afterlife, with status-based burial traditions.

segments.title: Safety coffins and premature burial fears
segments.summary: Eighteenth and nineteenth century safety coffins addressed fear of being buried alive (taphephobia). William Tebb's book documented premature burial cases. Count Carnicar patented a breathing tube with a signal flag. Dr. Timothy Clark Smith's grave has a glass viewing window.

segments.title: Expensive caskets, DIY coffins, and Mike Tyson's mother
segments.summary: The Promethean casket from Batesville can cost around $30,000 and was used for Michael Jackson and James Brown. DIY coffin plans are available online. Mike Tyson had his mother reburied in a better casket. Potter's fields are discussed, along with a visit to Mount Vernon.

segments.title: Listener mail from Peter
segments.summary: Peter in Virginia, a Georgia Tech fan, writes that the show helped him through a barium CT scan while being diagnosed with diffuse large B cell lymphoma. The hosts respond warmly and joke about Georgia rivalries.

segments.title: Sign-off and website reference
segments.summary: Hosts give social media and email contacts and promote the Jack Threads sponsor. They point to the how stuff works coffin article.
